segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Peter and John were going up to the temple for the hour of prayer, the ninth hour.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And a man who had been lame from his mother’s womb was being carried in, whom they set down every day at the temple gate called Beautiful to ask for alms from those going into the temple.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he saw Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asked to receive alms.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peter looked intently at him, as did John, and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Look at us.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He fixed his attention on them, expecting to receive something from them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Peter said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Silver and gold I do not have, but what I have, this I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, walk!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And grasping him by the right hand, he raised him up. Immediately his feet and ankles were made strong,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and leaping up, he stood and began to walk, and he went into the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And all the people saw him walking and praising God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they recognized him as the one who used to sit asking for alms at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, and they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While he clung to Peter and John, all the people ran together to them at the colonnade called Solomon’s, struck with wonder.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Peter saw this, he addressed the people:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Men of Israel, why are you marveling at this, or why do you look so intently at us, as though by our own power or piety we had made him walk?

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: The God of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his servant Jesus, whom you handed over and denied before Pilate, though he had decided to release him.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But you denied the Holy and Righteous One and asked for a murderer to be granted to you,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and you killed the author of life, whom God raised from the dead; of this we are witnesses.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And on the basis of faith in his name, his name has made strong this man whom you see and know; the faith that comes through him has given him this complete health in front of all of you.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did your rulers also.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But what God announced beforehand through the mouth of all the prophets, that his Messiah would suffer, he has fulfilled in this way.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Turn back, then, and return, that your sins may be wiped out,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: so that seasons of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord, and that he may send the Messiah appointed for you, Jesus,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: whom heaven must receive until the times of the restoration of all things, of which God spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets from of old.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Moses said, ‘The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You shall listen to him in everything he says to you.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And it will be that every person who does not listen to that prophet will be utterly destroyed from among the people.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And all the prophets who have spoken, from Samuel and those who came after him, also announced these days.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant that God made with your fathers, saying to Abraham, ‘And in your offspring all the families of the earth will be blessed.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: It was for you first that God raised up his servant and sent him to bless you by turning each of you away from your wicked ways.”

notes.note: Hours were counted from sunrise, so the ninth hour is about three in the afternoon. This was the time of the afternoon sacrifice in the temple and a customary time of prayer.
No other ancient source uses this name for a temple gate. It is often identified with a great bronze gate on the east side of the temple courts, but the identification is uncertain.

Many manuscripts read “rise up and walk.” The SBLGNT follows the shorter reading found in some of the earliest witnesses, on the view that the longer form was filled out from similar healing stories in the Gospels.

notes.traditional: his Son Jesus (KJV); his servant Jesus (most modern versions)
notes.note: The Greek word can mean either “child” or “servant.” Most scholars hold that “servant” is meant here, because “has glorified his servant” echoes the Greek of Isaiah 52:13, where the Lord’s servant is “glorified,” and because the same word is used of David as God’s servant in Acts 4:25. The same word recurs in verse 26.

notes.traditional: Prince of life (KJV); Author of life (most modern versions)
notes.note: The Greek word was used for a leader, a founder, or the originator of something. It can mean here either the one who is the source of life or the one who leads the way into life, and the Greek does not decide between them. “Author” is used in the sense of originator, in pointed contrast with “you killed.”

The Greek of this verse is awkward and literally reads “on the faith of his name.” Most interpreters take it as faith in the name of Jesus, but the text does not say whether the faith is that of the apostles, of the healed man, or both. “The faith that comes through him” most likely means faith that Jesus himself makes possible.

The Greek word means “anointed one” and here is a title for the king Israel expected, not a name. “Messiah” is used where the title is the point, as here and in verse 20, and “Christ” where the word is attached to “Jesus” as a name, as in verse 6. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

“Repent” now suggests mainly feeling sorry, whereas the Greek word carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep “repent” as an established term understood to include a change of life. The verb that follows it, “return,” is a different Greek word with a closely related meaning.

notes.phrase: the restoration of all things, of which God spoke
notes.note: The Greek can also be read as “the establishment of all that God spoke,” meaning the time when everything the prophets foretold comes to pass. The noun more usually means restoration to an earlier or proper state, and the related verb is used in Acts 1:6 of restoring the kingdom to Israel, so most translations render it as here.
Manuscripts vary here between “the Lord God,” “the Lord your God,” and “the Lord our God.” The SBLGNT prints the shortest form; the others are probably adjustments toward the wording of Deuteronomy.

notes.phrase: will be utterly destroyed from among the people
notes.note: Peter’s quotation in verses 22–23 draws on Deuteronomy 18:15–19, where Moses promises a prophet like himself. The warning here is worded in the language of Leviticus 23:29, which speaks of a person being cut off from the people. Combining related passages in this way was a common practice in Jewish citation of Scripture.

The verb is the same one used in verse 22 for God “raising up” a prophet, and most interpreters take it here in that sense: God brought Jesus onto the scene and sent him to Israel. It is also a regular word for raising from the dead, and some understand it of the resurrection. The rendering keeps the link with verse 22 and leaves both readings open.

candidates.reason: Used of Jesus in Acts 3:13, 3:26, 4:27, 4:30 and of David and Israel elsewhere, where translations split between “servant,” “child” and “Son,” and the Isaianic servant echo depends on a consistent choice.
Occurs at Acts 3:15, 5:31 and Hebrews 2:10, 12:2, where versions vary among “author,” “prince,” “leader,” “pioneer” and “founder,” and readers should be able to see it is one title.

With “turn back” assigned to μετανοέω, the frequent neighboring verb ἐπιστρέφω (“turn,” “return,” “turn to God”) needs a fixed rendering that stays distinct from it, especially where the two occur together as here and in Acts 26:20.
Recurs in Matthew 6, Luke 11–12 and Acts 9–10, 24; “alms” is traditional but dated, and alternatives such as “charity” or “gifts to the poor” would otherwise vary from chapter to chapter.

The Abrahamic promise is quoted across Acts, Romans, Galatians and Hebrews, and Paul’s argument from the singular in Galatians 3:16 requires one consistent choice among “seed,” “offspring” and “descendants.”
